vpnTunnel.summary:
The VPN tunnel has three separate problems. Each was measured on this PC against the repo's Go WireGuard test peer on 127.0.0.1. The peer was used two ways: loopback (no internet) and `-exit` mode, which forwards to the real internet. That reproduces the whole Lumen tunnel stack except the Proton WAN leg.

(1) The idle core is a busy-wait poll in the Samsung Emscripten glue. `___syscall168` in `wg-core.cjs` never blocks. It calls the shim's `poll(timeout 0)` for each fd in a loop until the 20 ms `POLL_MS` slice runs out. That is about 28,000 postMessage + Atomics.wait round trips per second at idle (1.04–1.07 cores). The UDP fd always answers POLLOUT, so the spin never sleeps. The glue already contains a blocking path (`SOCKFS.callPoll`); routing socket-only polls to it drops idle CPU to 0.02–0.04 cores with the same new-connection latency (7 ms median). No wasm rebuild is needed.

(2) "Heavy pages don't load properly" fits a hard limit in lwIP's in-tunnel DNS. With `DNS_TABLE_SIZE 8`, at most 8 lookups can be pending (duplicates count) and only 8 names are cached. Every extra concurrent CONNECT gets an immediate `vpn: dns-failed` 502, which Edge reports as `ERR_TUNNEL_CONNECTION_FAILED`. In tests, 30 concurrent CONNECTs to 15 hosts got 22 failures cold and 14 warm. 12 concurrent CONNECTs to one new host got 4 failures.

(3) Throughput is capped by the shim's per-syscall cross-thread round trip, not by wasm crypto. Each call costs 24–36 µs unloaded, with p99 85 µs. At 43 Mbit/s there are about 14,000 round trips per second: one per received packet, one per lwIP ACK, plus polls. Waiting on the bridge takes 76% of the tunnel worker's time; wasm itself takes about 8–10%. Under CPU contention a round trip averages 2.3 ms (p99 30 ms), and a 5 MB loopback download collapsed to a few KB/s with 16 s stalls. That fits heavy pages, where Edge rendering uses the CPU.

A JS-only prototype that batches UDP receives and sends without waiting raised 20-parallel throughput 2.5x on loopback and 1.75x to the internet. Against the internet, base Lumen did 48 Mbit/s on one stream versus 212 direct and 96 for a native wireguard-go client on the same peer.

Not caps: lwIP TCP_WND, mux credit and pbuf/MEM sizes. A 30-stream slow-consumer test completed fully and probes kept working.

Limits of these numbers:
- The live Lumen VPN was off (vpn.state "off", proxyPort null), so nothing was measured through the live proxy. I did not turn the owner's VPN on, and I did not start a second tunnel with the real config, because that could take over the live WireGuard session. The live process was confirmed idle: 16 ms of CPU in 10 s, 11 threads, no VPN worker.
- Other agents' Edge/Chrome processes had the machine at 100% CPU for long stretches. Where marked, I ran at High priority or in quiet windows and repeated runs. Throughput varies by about ±30% between runs.
- No repo files were changed. Scratch scripts and the prototype copies (base, instr, p1 = poll patch, p2 = +8 MiB rcvbuf, p3 = +batched UDP) are in C:/Users/pranj/AppData/Local/Temp/lumen-vpnperf-tunnel. Its `keys.json` holds throwaway keys made with `testpeer genkey`. Every Edge I started was killed, its temp profile was deleted, and the reference conf file was removed.

rootCauses.cause: The Samsung Emscripten glue implements poll() as a busy-wait. ___syscall168 loops over the fds, calling stream_ops.poll, which runs tizentvwasm poll([fd], 0) with all event bits (59), until the timeout runs out. wg_poll(POLL_MS=20) therefore makes hundreds of synchronous shim round trips per slice instead of one blocking wait. The I/O worker's readiness() always reports POLLOUT for UDP, so every probe returns 'ready' and nothing ever sleeps. The glue already has a blocking path (SOCKFS.callPoll, behind syscall168TizenSocketOnly), but ___syscall168 does not use it.
rootCauses.evidence: At idle: 27,914 poll(0) calls/s (ev=59, all ready, timeoutSum 0) against 50 wg_poll loops/s, and 1.04-1.07 cores. Routing socket-only polls to SOCKFS.callPoll (patch-poll.cjs) gave 33 polls/s, 0.02-0.04 cores and an unchanged 7 ms new-connection fetch. The live server showed 1 core busy when its VPN was on, matching the owner's report. That burned core also competes with Edge's renderer and screencast encoder.

rootCauses.cause: lwIP DNS inside the wasm is limited to DNS_TABLE_SIZE 8 (lwipopts.h), so DNS_MAX_REQUESTS is 8. At most 8 lookups can be pending, duplicates of one name each take a slot, and only 8 names are cached. mux.c handles a MUX_OPEN with a hostname by calling dns_gethostbyname. When it returns ERR_MEM, mux.c sends RST 'dns-failed', the proxy replies 502 'vpn: dns-failed', and Edge marks the resource ERR_TUNNEL_CONNECTION_FAILED. Heavy pages open many connections to many hosts at once, and Edge preconnects up to 6 per host.
rootCauses.evidence: 30 concurrent CONNECTs to 15 hosts: 22 failed cold, 14 failed warm. 12 distinct new hosts: exactly 8 OK, 4 failed. 12 copies of one new host: 8 OK, 4 failed; 12 OK once cached. The failures are immediate (14-57 ms). lwIP 2.2.1 dns.c dns_enqueue returns ERR_MEM when the table or request slots are full. One ERR_TUNNEL_CONNECTION_FAILED appeared in a real Edge load of theverge.com through the tunnel.

rootCauses.cause: Every socket syscall from the wasm is a synchronous cross-thread round trip (shim Bridge.call: postMessage, Atomics.wait, the I/O worker's event loop, reply, Atomics.notify), with structured clone, Array.from of the 60 control words, and an Error with a stack trace for each EAGAIN. A received WireGuard packet costs one round trip, and each ACK lwIP sends (about every 2 segments) costs another. The cost is two thread wake-ups per syscall, so it explodes under CPU contention.
rootCauses.evidence: 14,031 round trips/s at 43 Mbit/s; waiting on the bridge is 76% of the tunnel worker's time; wasm about 8-10%. A round trip is 24-36 us unloaded, but 2.4 ms mean / 32 ms p99 with the machine at 100% CPU, where a 5 MB loopback download crawled at about 3-4 KB/s with 16 s stalls. Base tunnel vs direct internet: 48 vs 212 Mbit/s single, 61 vs 120 Mbit/s for 20 parallel. A native wireguard-go client on the same peer did 96 Mbit/s. Prototype p3 (batched UDP recv, unacknowledged batched UDP send) cut UDP round trips by about 4x: 20-parallel 45-69 -> 125-188 Mbit/s loopback and 61 -> 107 internet; single stream 31-37 -> 47-60 loopback and 48 -> 59 internet.

rootCauses.cause: Because of the per-packet two-thread design (above) and the self-inflicted spinning core, the tunnel is very sensitive to CPU contention. A heavy page makes Edge use several cores, and the tunnel threads run at normal priority.
rootCauses.evidence: Bridge throughput: 422 calls/s at normal priority under load vs 10,854 at High priority under the same load. The tunnel start took 40 s (wasm ready at 22 s) under load, past the 15 s start timeout (vpn-start-timeout seen twice), against 0.6-0.9 s at High priority.

rootCauses.cause: The I/O worker's UDP socket uses the 64 KB default receive buffer, while a 706 KB lwIP TCP window lets about 500 datagrams arrive in one burst. At 160-210 Mbit/s line rate, 64 KB fills in about 3 ms, so any I/O-worker hiccup drops packets, and TCP backs off.
rootCauses.evidence: getRecvBufferSize() = 65536 by default; setRecvBufferSize(8 MiB) is accepted (8388608). No change on the zero-latency loopback, so the WAN effect is inferred, not measured.

rootCauses.cause: The poll waiter list grows without limit in the I/O worker once poll blocks (needed together with the poll fix). ops.poll pushes an evaluate closure onto every polled socket, and only wake() clears it. The idle mux socket receives no data from the hub, so its list grows by about 33 entries/s.
rootCauses.evidence: Code reading of tizentvwasm-io-worker.cjs ops.poll / wake(). With the current spin it does not happen, because every poll returns 'ready' immediately.

rootCauses.cause: Small per-packet overheads: readStatus() runs at every wg_poll (malloc, snprintf of JSON in wasm, JSON.parse; 50-700/s); SockError captures a stack for each EAGAIN; the glue allocates a temporary Uint8Array per recv. The hub receives one 1.3-1.4 KB DATA frame per lwIP pbuf (thousands/s), each pushed and written separately. TunnelStream.push ignores backpressure (up to 1 MiB of credit per stream is buffered on the main thread). encodeFrame copies upload payloads, and Buffer.concat in the decoder only runs for frames that span chunks.
rootCauses.evidence: Profiles: readStatus 1.2%, SockError 2.0-4.5%, getErrorCode 1.1-1.8% of the tunnel worker; main thread 73-83% idle with writev 4.5-7.4%. The slow-consumer test buffered 67 MB on the hub/proxy side.

rootCauses.cause: Not caps at present (checked): lwIP TCP_WND 706 KB, TCP_SND_BUF, MUX_INITIAL_CREDIT 1 MiB, MEM_SIZE 12 MiB and the pbuf pool. All rx pbufs are PBUF_RAM, so PBUF_POOL_SIZE 6144 is unused. Proxy piping and the main thread are also not a cap. A separate browser-side limit that I did not verify here: Chromium allows at most 32 sockets per proxy server for all traffic through --proxy-server.
rootCauses.evidence: Slow-consumer run: 30 paused x 4 MB streams completed with probes still working. A single stream on a zero-RTT loopback is limited by processing, not window (47-60 Mbit/s with p3). The main thread is mostly idle in profiles. At 60 ms RTT the window still allows about 94 Mbit/s per stream.

plan.change: Make poll block for real. Add a 10th glue anchor (same post-processing step as tools/patch-glue.cjs, recorded in NOTICE.md). In ___syscall168, right after reading fds/nfds/timeout, insert: if(nfds>0&&SOCKFS.countFDsInPollFDs(fds,nfds).sockets===nfds){return SOCKFS.callPoll(fds,nfds,timeout)}. In the same change, fix the I/O worker poll so a finished poll removes its evaluate closure from every socket's waiters (for example a per-poll token checked and spliced on timeout and on completion). Optionally also skip the per-loop readStatus() unless 250 ms have passed.
plan.expectedGain: Idle CPU about 1.05 -> 0.02-0.04 cores (measured with p1); new-connection latency unchanged (7 ms median); frees a core for Edge rendering and the screencast at all times
plan.risk: Low. The glue's own callPoll is used, wasm is unchanged, readiness bits are mapped by the glue's pollFlagsMap. Without the waiter cleanup, memory leaks at idle. Verify with test/vpn.test.js and test/browser-vpn.test.js.

plan.change: Add a JS-side resolver in front of OPEN in wireguard.js connect(). Keep a hostname -> IPv4 cache (60-300 s, dropped after a failed open). Deduplicate in-flight lookups per name. Run at most 6 concurrent T.DNS lookups so lwIP's 8 slots are never exceeded. Retry once after 50-100 ms on an empty DNSANSWER. Then send OPEN 'port:ip'. The hostname still reaches the far side in TLS SNI and the Host header, because only the dial target changes. Optional: rebuild the wasm with DNS_TABLE_SIZE 32-64; NOTICE says the Samsung emsdk build in the worktree reproduces byte for byte.
plan.expectedGain: Removes the dns-failed RSTs: 22/30 failed CONNECTs cold and 14/30 warm, down to 0 expected. Saves one in-tunnel DNS round trip to Proton per new connection on a cache hit (lwIP's 8-entry cache thrashes on heavy pages). Directly targets 'heavy pages don't load properly'.
plan.risk: Low-medium. No TTL from lwIP (use a short fixed TTL and refresh when a dial fails). Status counts and 'vpn-dns-*' error codes should stay the same for the UI.

plan.change: Cut UDP round trips in the shim, as in prototype p3. (a) recvFrom on a nonblocking UDP fd is served from a local queue, filled by one 'recvmany' round trip that packs up to 64 datagrams [u16 len][u16 port][4 ip][payload] into the shared buffer. (b) sendTo on UDP is queued locally and flushed as one 'sendbatch' postMessage (transferring the buffers) before the next synchronous call, or at 128 items / 512 KB. (c) poll reports POLLIN for fds with queued datagrams and then probes the others with timeout 0. Also throw cached errno objects without a stack for EAGAIN, and replace s.rx.shift() with a head index.
plan.expectedGain: Measured: 20-parallel x 1 MB 45-69 -> 125-188 Mbit/s loopback (about 2.5x) and 61 -> 107 Mbit/s internet via the exit peer (1.75x). Single stream 31-37 -> 47-60 Mbit/s loopback and 48 -> 59 internet. UDP round trips drop from about 9,400/s to about 1,400/s at a similar rate.
plan.risk: Medium. UDP send errors become asynchronous (the current code already replies payload.length before the send callback). postMessage FIFO keeps ordering with later synchronous ops. MSG_PEEK and TCP paths are unchanged. The shim is a vendored third_party file, so record the change in NOTICE.

plan.change: Structural fix: drop the I/O worker. Let the tunnel worker own the dgram/net sockets and give the shim synchronous calls over local queues, where poll never blocks. Drive wg_poll(0) from events: setImmediate-coalesced on UDP 'message' or mux 'data', plus a 10-25 ms timer while streams are open (about 100-250 ms idle) for sys_check_timeouts. Resolve a hostname endpoint in JS before wg_start (gethostbyname is the only blocking call). Next step: replace the loopback-TCP hub link with a MessagePort or SharedArrayBuffer ring and coalesce DATA frames per stream before push().
plan.expectedGain: Removes the remaining about 2,900 synchronous round trips/s (bridge waiting is still 56% of the tunnel worker in p3). Estimated: single stream close to the wireguard-go reference on this machine (96 Mbit/s internet, 81-85 loopback); parallel up to the link (110-210 Mbit/s direct). Throughput would no longer collapse under CPU contention, since a packet would no longer need two thread wake-ups. These are estimates; I did not build a prototype.
plan.risk: Medium-high. A larger rewrite of vendored code: nonblocking connect/EINPROGRESS and SO_ERROR emulation, sockets that bind asynchronously, and an extra event loop in the tunnel worker. Needs the full VPN test suite plus soak and rekey tests (tools/scratch/review-vpn-robustness scripts).

plan.change: After ensureUdp's 'listening', call setRecvBufferSize(8 MiB) and setSendBufferSize(1 MiB) on the I/O worker's UDP socket (or the tunnel worker's, after the structural fix). Optionally raise Lumen's process priority with os.setPriority(PRIORITY_ABOVE_NORMAL) at startup, once fix 1 has made the tunnel idle-cheap.
plan.expectedGain: Fewer burst drops (and less TCP backoff) on the real Proton path at 100-200 Mbit/s; this cannot be measured on loopback. Under contention, High priority made bridge calls 25x faster (422 -> 10,854 calls/s) and start 30x faster; ABOVE_NORMAL should land in between.
plan.risk: Low for the buffers. Low-medium for priority: Lumen must not starve Edge, which is why it comes after fix 1.

plan.change: Hub and stream small fixes: coalesce consecutive DATA payloads per stream within one socket chunk before TunnelStream.push. Respect push() returning false: delay CREDIT and stop buffering past about 256 KB per stream. Add a fast path in encodeFrame for Buffers (header in a separate small Buffer plus socket.cork/writev, no payload copy). Keep a single pending chunk in the decoder instead of repeated Buffer.concat for straddling frames.
plan.expectedGain: A few % of main-thread CPU now; it matters more once the tunnel is about 3x faster (thousands of 1.4 KB frames/s). Also bounds memory with 250 streams (now up to 1 MiB of credit each on the main thread).
plan.risk: Low. The frame protocol is unchanged and the decoder is unit-tested in test/vpn.test.js.

pageLoad.summary:
Heavy pages fail or load slowly over the VPN for four separate reasons. I measured each one with my own tunnel and proxy on data/vpn/wg.conf, because the live VPN was off the whole time (vpn.enabled=false, so there was no live proxy port). Every one of my runs checked that the live VPN stayed off.

(1) The machine was at 100% CPU on all 16 logical cores. The load came from browsers other agents leaked: 147 chrome.exe processes using 12.8 cores (about 17 headless Chrome instances under %TEMP%/lumen-review/cdp*) and 167 msedge.exe processes using 3.7 cores (stale lumen-shot-* Edges). The VPN engine routes every socket call through postMessage + Atomics.wait, so it collapsed: 4-10 KB/s, TLS handshakes of 4-16 s, a 7-15 s fetch for a tiny google.com/generate_204 page, and the tunnel took 8-9 s to come up. After the leaked browsers were cleaned up, the same path ran at 1.2-2.9 MB/s. Over the same period the live Browser showed "Microsoft Edge did not start in time".

(2) Running the VPN process at AboveNormal priority restores full speed under CPU contention: 0.47-0.71 MB/s becomes 2.25-2.51 MB/s. A bigger UDP receive buffer does not help.

(3) wg-core's lwIP DNS table holds only 8 entries. With more than 8 lookups in flight, the extra ones fail instantly (about 5 ms) with dns-failed, and Edge shows that as ERR_TUNNEL_CONNECTION_FAILED. In a burst of 30 real hostnames, 22 failed. Every CNN load lost 5 real hosts this way, including CNN's own lightning.cnn.com and registry.api.cnn.io. The cache also keeps only 8 names, so each lookup beyond that costs about 80 ms again. A prototype fix in a scratch copy of proxy.js resolves names in JS (at most 6 lookups at a time, same-name lookups shared, TTL cache) and then dials the IP. With it, these instant failures dropped to 0; only the Proton DNS filter's ad and tracker blocks were left.

(4) Smaller causes:
- lwIP's 3 s first SYN retransmit (the initial TCP retry timeout) made 3-4 tunnel opens per 5-page cycle stall for 3.07-3.36 s.
- Lumen acks every screencast frame immediately, so Edge encodes 32-53 fps on animated pages while Lumen forwards at most 15. That wastes about 0.3-0.5 of a core per page, compared with spacing the acks 66 ms apart.
- Proton's NetShield DNS filter blocks about 25-37 ad and tracker hosts per CNN load, plus brunhild.challenges.cloudflare.com.
- Through the VPN, vimeo.com/watch is stuck on Cloudflare's "Just a moment... Verify to continue" page: 8 requests, against 445 requests loaded directly.

What is not the problem: the proxy's limits (real pages peaked at 93-107 streams against the cap of 250, with no busy refusals or evictions), Edge's own queue before connecting (p90 at most 263 ms), and the Edge flags. --disable-quic is required, HTTP/2 works through CONNECT, and the 226 MB profile is normal.

The main fixes, in order: run the Lumen process at AboveNormal priority, stop the leaked browsers, add the JS DNS limiter and cache to proxy.js, space out the screencast acks, then rebuild wg-core with a larger DNS table and a 1 s first retry.

All scripts are in C:/Users/pranj/AppData/Local/Temp/lumen-pageload. The prototype is vpnmod/proxy.js there; no repo files were changed. Every Edge I started was killed and its temp profile deleted.

rootCauses.cause: The engine is CPU-bound and every socket call hops between threads (postMessage + Atomics.wait to the I/O worker, about 1.5 cores per 42 Mbit/s), so throughput collapses when the host CPU is contended. The host was saturated by leaked headless Chrome/Edge instances from other agents' runs.
rootCauses.evidence: At 100% CPU: VPN 3.7-10 KB/s, TLS 4-16 s, tunnel up in 8-9 s, while the syscall bridge fell from 53.9k to 1.8k calls/s (p99 0.047 to 11.3 ms). After the cleanup: 1.2-2.9 MB/s. Controlled 2-core contention: 0.47-0.71 MB/s at Normal priority vs 2.25-2.51 MB/s at AboveNormal.

rootCauses.cause: wg-core lwIP DNS_TABLE_SIZE is 8 (lwipopts.h). A 9th lookup in flight gets ERR_MEM, which mux.c turns into RST 'dns-failed'; the proxy answers 502 and Edge shows ERR_TUNNEL_CONNECTION_FAILED. The 8-entry cache also forces about 80 ms re-lookups on busy pages.
rootCauses.evidence: Burst of 30 distinct names: 22 failed in 5 ms. Every CNN load had 5 instant (<20 ms) dns-failed on hosts that resolve fine one at a time (lightning.cnn.com 95 ms, registry.api.cnn.io 75 ms, cdn.optimizely.com 71 ms). With the JS limiter/cache prototype these overflow failures went to 0.

rootCauses.cause: lwIP's initial TCP retry timeout (LWIP_TCP_RTO_TIME default 3000 ms) and its DNS retry timer turn any single lost SYN or DNS packet into a stall of about 3 s.
rootCauses.evidence: 3-4 tunnel opens per 5-page cycle took 3.07-3.36 s (4 simultaneous opens to upload.wikimedia.org at 3073-3079 ms); tunnel open p99 3.07 s against p50 110-158 ms.

rootCauses.cause: Screencast frames are acked to Edge immediately (browser.js onScreencastFrame), so Edge JPEG-encodes every compositor frame (32-53 fps) while Lumen forwards at most 15 fps. That CPU competes with the page and the VPN engine.
rootCauses.evidence: CNN over a 20 s cap: browser process 28-34 CPU-s with immediate ack, 23-24.5 s with acks 66 ms after each frame, 11-11.6 s with no screencast; frames generated 700-1167 vs about 480.

rootCauses.cause: External to Lumen: Proton's NetShield DNS filter blocks ad/tracker hosts, including the Cloudflare challenge host, and the VPN exit IP draws Cloudflare bot challenges, so some pages never render through the VPN.
rootCauses.evidence: 25-37 NetShield dns-failed answers per CNN load at 50-230 ms (a real round trip), including brunhild.challenges.cloudflare.com. vimeo.com/watch through the VPN: title 'Just a moment...', text 'Verify to continue', 8 requests; direct: 445 requests, the real page.

rootCauses.cause: Each new connection costs much more through the tunnel (CONNECT, then in-tunnel DNS, then lwIP TCP, then TLS), and nothing reuses DNS answers across connections beyond lwIP's 8 names.
rootCauses.evidence: Edge new-connection time p50 450-773 ms through the VPN vs 41-100 ms direct; TTFB p50 121-505 ms vs 29-185 ms.

rootCauses.cause: proxy.js only frees a slot by evicting a tunnel that has been idle for at least 2 s, so requests beyond 250 streams wait 2-3 s. Real pages did not get there.
rootCauses.evidence: Synthetic 300 + 40 CONNECTs: 90 evictions, waiters 2.0-2.9 s. Real pages peaked at 93-107 streams with 0 evictions or busy refusals.

phoneRender.summary: Phone-side rendering is a real, measurable part of the choppiness, and it is concentrated in the frame path of web/js/views/browser.js (onFrame/draw, lines ~401-445). There are three problems. (1) The base64-to-bytes step `Uint8Array.from(atob(data), (c) => c.charCodeAt(0))` (line 426) costs 36 ms (p50) / 57 ms (p95) of main-thread time for each 1280x720 frame and 11 ms for each phone-sized frame on a 4x-throttled emulated phone. It also creates 4.7 MB / 1.4 MB of garbage per frame, about 33 times the JPEG size. `Uint8Array.fromBase64` does the same work in 1.1 ms / 0.6 ms with almost no garbage. (2) Frames are acked only after decode and draw, and the server allows only UNACKED_LIMIT=2 frames in flight. That puts the phone's processing time inside the flow-control loop: in replay the server skipped 120-183 of roughly 300 frames per 20 s and sent only 4-7 fps. Acking on receipt raised that to 11-13 fps and cut skips to 14-37 on a good link. (3) There is a freeze bug, reproduced. If one frame fails to decode while another is queued, neither is acked and the queued frame is never drawn. The server then has 2 outstanding frames and stops sending to that phone until the view or visibility changes: 0 frames were sent or drawn in the remaining ~10 s, against 111 sent and 93 drawn with the fix. That fits 'heavy pages don't load properly' as a frozen picture. Other parts are fine. Canvas sizing is not oversized: the backing equals the frame (356x466 at DPR 1 for a phone viewport, 1280x720 only while the TV/desktop viewport holds). drawImage takes under 0.5 ms. createImageBitmap decodes off the main thread in Chromium (worst main-thread gap 2.7 ms while decoding). JSON.parse of the frame message takes 0.3 ms. The service worker never touches /live. There is no per-frame DOM work apart from the first frame, frame-size changes, and a once-per-second meta update. Caveat: the host PC was at 100% CPU the whole time (Defender 235%, ~180 msedge and ~120 chrome processes from other agents), and headless rAF stalled for seconds under that load. So treat absolute fps and latency as noisy. The per-frame CPU, allocation and long-task differences are large and consistent in every run. I could not measure WebKit/JSC on a real iPhone; check with Safari Web Inspector Timeline. Scratch harness: C:\Users\pranj\AppData\Local\Temp\lumen-phone-bench (no repo files changed; every Edge I started was killed and its temp profiles deleted).

rootCauses.cause: Frames are acked only after decode and draw (browser.js:413-414) while the server allows 2 unacked frames (server/features/browser.js:20, 327-333). The phone's decode, draw and main-thread queueing sit inside the flow-control loop, so the server keeps skipping this phone.

rootCauses.cause: Freeze: if createImageBitmap rejects (corrupt or truncated data, or iOS memory pressure) while another frame is queued, the catch at browser.js:418 leaves both unacked and the queued frame undrawn. The server then has 2 outstanding frames and never sends to that client again until a view or visibility change resets its watcher (browser.js:394-401 server side).
rootCauses.evidence: bench3.mjs stall test: baseline ackedCorrupt=false, ackedFollower=false, 0 frames sent or drawn after the event for ~10 s; prototype keeps going (111 sent, 93 drawn). Code: onFrame's try/catch skips the ack and leaves `queued` set.

rootCauses.cause: Decode and draw are strictly serial, and every received frame is drawn in arrival order. There is no 'newest only' at decode time and no rAF alignment, so a burst queues work and the picture lags.
rootCauses.evidence: Baseline produced-to-drawn p50 / p95: 555 / 1171 ms (phone frames, good link, contended host) vs 144 / 226 ms with newest-only plus rAF. screencast.summary:
Screencast pipeline investigation, with numbers from my own dev stacks and headless Edges. Nothing in the repo was changed; scratch scripts are in C:/Users/pranj/AppData/Local/Temp/lumen-sc-bench.

What Lumen does today (server/features/browser.js, config defaults):
- Screencast settings: Page.startScreencast format=jpeg, quality=60, maxWidth=1280, maxHeight=800, everyNthFrame=1.
- Every Edge frame is acked immediately. Fan-out is capped at maxFps=15 (5 fps when the bytes repeat).
- Phones get the frame as JSON text (base64 inside) on the shared /live socket. Each phone may have at most 2 unacked frames (UNACKED_LIMIT=2), and it acks only after painting.
- The TV gets raw JPEG bytes with no ack. A frame is skipped only when the socket's bufferedAmount is above 384 KB.
- While the TV is attached the single stream is 1280x720, and every phone gets that too.

Causes of choppiness, in order of evidence:
1. The 2-frame ack window serialises on the Wi-Fi round trip. Phone fps is roughly min(15, 2/(RTT+decode)): 14.4 fps falls to 10.8 with 100 ms added ack delay and to 5.8 with 250 ms. Even in perfect conditions the phone never exceeds 15 fps, which looks choppy when scrolling.
2. With the TV on, phones receive 1280x720 frames: 86-127 KB messages instead of 25-37 KB at their own 358x467 viewport.
3. The phone turns base64 into bytes with Uint8Array.from(atob(s), fn). That costs 24.6 ms per 63 KB frame at 4x CPU throttle, against 2 ms for a plain loop, 0.5 ms for Uint8Array.fromBase64 and 0 ms for binary frames. With the TV on and a 4x-slower phone CPU this produced roughly 60-90 ms long tasks on most frames (63 of ~64 in the loaded run, 30 of 115 on CNN), 6.4 painted fps and glass-to-glass latency of 301 ms p50 / 1.19 s max on the loaded PC. Those long tasks also delay touch handling.
4. Immediate acks make Edge encode 92-93 fps (canvas animation) or 30-54 fps (CNN), of which Lumen sends at most 15. That waste costs Edge about 1-2 cores and Node 11-33%. Under CPU contention the capture path is the first thing starved: the page still rendered at 69-90 frames/s while the screencast fell to 0.4-8 fps with 120-2700 ms lag.
5. The TV path has no flow control. A TV reading at 300 KB/s saw frames 3.0 s old (p50; p90 3.4 s), with 18 frames queued in the 384 KB Node buffer plus kernel buffers.

Does the slowest consumer throttle everyone? No. Each phone has its own window: an 80 ms decoder got 11.9 fps while the others got 14.4, and a slow TV left the phone at 14.5 fps. The real coupling is the shared 1280x720 stream while the TV is attached.

Ranked fixes:
- (a) Send phone frames as binary, which removes base64 decoding and 33% of the bytes.
- (b) Pace Edge at the source with held "token" acks. Prototype: Edge CPU fell from about 150% to 50-58% and Node from 11-17% to 2-4%, with similar frame freshness.
- (c) Replace the after-paint 2-frame window with ack-on-receipt plus a byte/time window, a timeout for stuck acks, and per-client fps.
- (d) Give the TV real flow control (screen-ack, or one frame in flight).
- (e) Run a second CDP screencast session for phones at phone size (verified: two independent screencasts on one tab, 93 fps each).
- (f) Adaptive JPEG quality and size caps.

Caveats:
- This PC was intermittently at 100% CPU from about 17 other agents' headless Chromes. Runs taken while it was idle are marked as such. The loaded runs are noisy but they show how badly the capture path collapses under CPU pressure.
- Mistake on my side: one cleanup command killed msedge.exe processes matching *lumen-test-* as well as my own *lumen-sc-edge-*. Some of those may have belonged to other agents' test stacks (28 processes in total). After that I only killed Edge by my own exact markers. All my Edge processes and temp profiles are gone.
- I did not touch the live Lumen server, the TV, or the VPN.
